problem: The unit check for Weber number is wrong. ρV²D gives kg/m³ × m²/s² × m = kg/s² = N/m, not kg/(m·s²) = Pa. Pa is the unit of ρV² alone (before multiplying by D). As written, a student checking units would find the ratio is not dimensionless.
fix: ρV² is in Pa; multiplying by D (m) gives Pa·m = N/m, the same unit as σ. So We = (N/m)/(N/m) is a pure number. Re is (m/s × m)/(m²/s), also unit-free.

problem: The factor is inverted. If a book uses Eu = Δp/(ρV²), then Eu = Δp/(2 × ½ρV²), so its value is half the value obtained with the definition used in this chapter, not twice it.
fix: Some books define Eu = Δp/(ρV²); with that definition every Eu is half the value used here (the value here is twice as large).

problem: The inequality sign is missing: 'Fr  1 is supercritical' has no comparison, so the student cannot tell whether the limit is above or below 1.
fix: Fr > 1 is supercritical. Fr < 1 is subcritical. Fr = 1 is critical.

problem: The subscripts m and p are never defined, and 'force a fixed length scale and fluid' is vague — the actual result is that, with the same fluid, both groups can be matched only at full scale (length ratio 1).
fix: Define m as model and p as prototype. Then: Re matching gives V_m/V_p = L_p/L_m, Fr matching gives V_m/V_p = √(L_m/L_p). If the same fluid is used, both hold together only when L_m = L_p, that is, the model must be full size; otherwise one group must be sacrificed or a different fluid used.

problem: Froude and Mach are the square roots of force ratios (Fr² = inertia ÷ gravity, Ma² = inertia ÷ elastic force), not direct force ratios, while the table lists all five as simple ratios of two forces.
fix: Keep the formulas Fr = V/√(gL) and Ma = V/c, but read them as inertia ÷ gravity and inertia ÷ elasticity in square-root form, exactly as Eu is a pressure ratio.
